### The blocked screen now tells you what happened
Until now every block looked the same: one screen, one message, whether you had run out of time on a site, opened something your organisation blocks, or reached for something you had asked to be kept away from.
It is a new screen, and it says which of those it was. Adult and gambling sites carry a reminder from the Qur'an. A spent daily limit says your time is up and that the site opens again tomorrow — nothing more, because running out of minutes is not something to be lectured about. A site your organisation blocks says so, and points you at your administrator. The same screen now appears for a blocked app as for a blocked site, in light and dark to match your Mac.
**Go back** now closes the tab instead of stepping through your history.
### Signing out clears the Mac
A Mac has no separate space per person, so block lists, schedules, limits, your habits, your usage history and your PIN all belonged to whoever was signed in — and stayed behind for whoever signed in next.
Signing out now clears them and returns the app to first-run setup. Two things survive on purpose: the Safe Internet DNS profile, which you consented to by name and which protects you signed in or out, and this Mac's place against your account's device limit, so signing in again does not use up another slot.
This applies to signing out yourself. Being signed out by an expired session leaves everything exactly where it was.
